abstractText:
COVID-19 continues to pose a daunting challenge that requires effective use of science to manage community response and recovery. The goals of this project are to apply community engagement principles in a series of virtual workshops hosted in partnership with local communities around Washington State that will respond directly to local needs for scientific discourse about COVID-19. These workshops will facilitate the exchange of knowledge and sharing of experiences in science-informed decision making and help local scientists understand how to apply their expertise to inform decisionmakers. The outcomes of this project will increase the understanding of how to use local-level science-for-policy discourse to address critical issues within and beyond the current pandemic management and recovery across the state and the country.

This project centers around a series of virtual workshops co-designed and co-created with local decisionmakers, community leaders, and participating scientists in diverse parts of Washington State. These workshops will be designed to cultivate cross-sector and multidisciplinary dialogues with scientists and local communities about key issues identified by community leaders related to the COVID-19 pandemic response and recovery. This project will advance knowledge in participatory design and public engagement around science for policy. The project’s co-design and engagement processes will create a replicable approach for providing greater science-for-policy discourse and innovation at the state and local levels.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
It has never been more important to integrate science effectively and sensitively into public discourse and decision-making. The COVID-19 pandemic has had widespread effects throughout every aspect of life and society. The pandemic response has required leaders in every sector and at national, state and local levels to take in information and assess options and tradeoffs to make decisions. This can be an extraordinary challenge in the face of a constantly evolving situation. Effective use of science continues to be needed to manage and recover from the COVID-19 pandemic. Community engagement expands the societal benefits of science by increasing the usefulness of scientific results, the application of science to inform policy, and the effectiveness of science communication.

The Washington State Academy of Sciences (WSAS) hosted virtual workshops co-designed and co-created with local decisionmakers, community leaders, and participating scientists in diverse parts of Washington State. The workshops cultivated cross-sector and multidisciplinary dialogues with scientists and local communities about key issues identified by community leaders related to the COVID-19 pandemic response and recovery. The dialogue events and their planning process facilitated the exchange of knowledge and sharing of experiences, to the benefit of communities, local decisionmakers, and local scientists.

One workshop, a dialogue with communities in Spokane, WA, considered ?How can a community grow in ways that enhance health?? The other dialogue with Coastal Washington communities investigated ?How does housing contribute to a thriving community?? The topics, panels, and questions were derived directly from the input of community members and participants. Throughout each dialogue event, panelists fielded questions and built on or responded to each other?s statements, often highlighting the interconnectedness of the issues at hand and bringing in the context of broader social issues,

The outcomes of the workshop series were:

  • Increased awareness among decisionmakers about emerging science relevant for local decision-making.
  • Increased awareness among scientists of state and local needs for scientific information.
  • Thoughtful dialogue focused on interconnectedness and shared community experiences.
  • Refined community engagement activities and processes that can be further developed as infrastructure to deepen the ongoing use of science in support of local needs, across the U.S.
  • Formation of new collaborations that persist after the workshop series, which enhance the use of science in local problem-solving.

More about the participants and the content of the discussions can be in summaries produced by WSAS: https://washacad.org/covid-19-community-dialogues/. Community planning partners were integral to disseminating the results of the workshops with their networks. The broader impacts of this project were improved science communication and expansion of the societal benefits of scientific activity. These impacts were achieved through the dialogue process, which facilitated the exchange of knowledge and sharing of experiences among researchers and community members with different types of expertise and experience. In addition to reaching the those who attended the events, the impact of the dialogue planning process catalyzed connections within communities, and across sectors and roles.

Our work advanced knowledge in participatory design and public engagement around science for policy. WSAS has developed an adaptable framework for further engagement and co-design processes, resulting in a replicable approach for building new relationships and providing greater science-for-policy discourse at the local level. This approach can be applied in future activities in response to the needs of communities across Washington State and the nation to find science-based solutions to challenging issues.

abstractText:
The Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) program in Physics and Astronomy at Washington State University (WSU) provides students advanced 10-week research internships that demonstrate how the concept of waves pervades all aspects of our physical universe. These internships will take place in world-class facilities under the direct supervision of faculty who are experts in their respective disciplines and highly experienced undergraduate research mentors. Recruitment and support for underrepresented and underserved groups in STEM are a significant focus of the program. This includes a major partnership with the NSF-funded Louis Stokes Alliance for Minority Participation (LSAMP) program at WSU. Peer and team mentoring and professional development are integral parts of the holistic experience within both the research setting and living experience. This is achieved in part through the WSU Community of Scholars program that includes scholars in all REU programs on campus (involving approximately 80 REU scholars each summer) and uniquely engenders relationships and networking opportunities with student peers across the country. This REU program will host 6-10 scholars each summer to foster their research skills and post-graduate career opportunities in physics, astronomy, and related fields to help create the next generation of STEM leaders.  

This REU program will provide undergraduate students with internships in world-class research groups spanning fields that include gravity waves, shock physics, low-dimensional and complex materials, and quantum atomic phenomena. Each student will select a project of interest from within the department and be paired with a faculty mentor who has extensive experience mentoring WSU undergraduates. State-of-the-art research facilities available include the Institute of Shock Physics, the WSU Dodgen Research Nuclear Reactor, the Center for Materials Research, the Franceschi Microscopy Center, and multiple Bose-Einstein Condensate instruments, including one on the International Space Station. Individual projects will be connected through the common concept of waves. Seminars in each subfield will be presented to all trainees to highlight this pervasive and connective physics and astronomy phenomenon. Professional development field trips to the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and the Hanford Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory will give students a broad experience of research settings, engage in meaningful discussions with researchers, and get insights into career opportunities. A University-wide, summer “Community of Scholars” program at WSU provides an interdisciplinary and social living environment and professional development opportunities for numerous REU and REU-like summer programs to engender social and professional relationships among its typically 80 undergraduate participants. This is of strategic importance to develop a network of peer support among students and is particularly important for underrepresented STEM disciplines groups. A partnership with the NSF-LSAMP program will synergize recruitment and support for underrepresented and underserved scholars.

projectOutComesReport:
This Research Experience for Undergraduates (REU) program provided 10-week paid research internships in physics and astronomy for promising undergraduate students interested in STEM research careers in the summers of 2021, 2022, and 2023. The program focused on providing these opportunities to students who did not have access to research opportunities in their home colleges and thus provided them with crucial skills, experience, and a professional network to be accepted and succeed in graduate school and become the next generation of United States leaders in STEM research.

The program created and produced the Art of Research Workshop which trained interns on important lab skills not taught in classes such as how to keep a lab notebook, how to read a research paper, and ethical practices in science as well as science communication skills such as how to write an abstract, give an elevator talk, and design a scientific poster. Students also toured major research facilities both at Washington State University (WSU) as well as the NSF’s Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO). Students gained an historical perspective of science on society through a tour of the Hanford B-reactor that produced the nation’s plutonium for the atomic bomb in World War II. Finally, “Waves in Physics” seminars were presented to show how the concept and mathematics of waves pervades all research areas in physics and astronomy. The REU program had a broader impact in that these activities were opened to those beyond the REU interns, for example, WSU students completing summer research as well as an independent internship program at the Institute for Shock Physics at WSU.

Each student completed an individual research project and presented their work in an all-University poster symposium at the end of the summer along with many other undergraduate researchers across different STEM programs. Additionally, 40% of the REU interns later presented their work at national conferences and three students published their work in peer-reviewed scientific journals with the extended mentorship of their WSU faculty mentors after the summer was over. Of those who have graduated, the majority (80%) have gone on to graduate school in a STEM field with the remaining starting their career in industry.

abstractText:
One of the populations hardest hit during an emerging epidemic are frontline healthcare workers. Infections in healthcare workers and in healthcare settings produce two separate but related challenges. The first, and most obvious, is that sick or dying healthcare workers cannot care for patients, causing labor shortages right at the moment when demand on a healthcare system is likely increasing due to the epidemic. The second problem is that, because of how difficult it is to control infections within hospitals, the epidemic itself can accelerate once it reaches the healthcare system, causing a rapid increase in the number of cases. Examples of this phenomena, which we call “nosocomial amplification”, are common, including both previous major coronavirus epidemics before COVID-19 (SARS and MERS) as well as Ebola. This project will seek to model and understand what factors within a hospital can prevent this from happening, to increase the resilience of healthcare systems. Outcomes from this effort will be informing behavioral guidelines for healthcare systems. Other broader impacts from this project include training and professional development opportunities for students.

	The researchers will adapt an existing model of within-hospital infection transmission to COVID-19 and combine this model with a spatially explicit agent-based model of the healthcare facilities in the state of North Carolina. This approach allows for the representation both of the healthcare environment, as well as the community where initial cases are seeded, where healthcare workers can infect – and be infected by – their community, etc. It also allows for the modeling of facility-level impacts of state-level decisions and allows us to address the question of how to best protect the health of both patients and healthcare workers in an environment where both are at significant risk of infection and critical supplies such as PPE are not necessarily unlimited. Simultaneously, they will collect data from hospitals in the SHEA Research Network on the changes brought on to staffing and clinical practice from COVID-19, such as whether or not the ratio of nurses to patients has changed, as well as ascertaining to what extent modeling has been used in hospital decision making, and whether or not it has been useful in that role. This project will thus have both a robust and sophisticated model for the interaction between hospitals at a granular level and the surrounding community, as well as timely parameter estimates from a diverse array of hospitals on how COVID-19 has changed their practices, as well as how modeling might be better tailored to inform the control of both COVID-19 and future epidemics.

program: RAPID, COVID-19 Research
projectOutComesReport:
This project focused on understanding how the healthcare system can potentially exacerbate, or even cause, outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases. While this phenomenon has been observed for some pathogens, like MERS and Ebola, it is not well defined or understood. Our project has established a mathematical framework to examine this concept, which we call "nosocomial amplification" as the first step toward understanding and mitigating it. This has included both published papers and papers currently being prepared examining the interplay between the healthcare system and the community for COVID-19, as well as a more general framework for multiple pathogens, exploring the implications for controlling emerging infectious diseases. Additionally, during the COVID-19 pandemic, we examined a related phenomenon, "carceral amplification", estimating the role jails and detention centers might play in propogating COVID-19 in the communities they serve. The results of that portion of the project were used to help inform the justice system and policy makers into the means by which the normal operation of jails might be adjusted to reduce the threat of COVID-19 not only to incarcerated persons, but also to jail staff and other employees of the criminal justice system, as well as the general public.

Alongside this, the project also surveyed hospitals who were members of the Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America (SHEA) Research Network. This survey was intended to help understand what changes hospitals made to staffing and other policies during the pandemic. For example, if they used travel nurses, changed staffing ratios, or discontinued certain in-person activities. The results of this survey will help inform future models of hospitals during pandemics, to ensure that the results of models used to study hospital-based transmission are based on real-world, on-the-ground conditions. This survey also included several answers on how modeling as used by hospitals during the pandemic, including who hospitals worked with for their modeling needs, who had access to these models, what sorts of activities were modeled, and who had access to the results of those models. It also included a free text field where survey respondants could discuss their experiences using modeling in hospitals. This portion of the survey is being analyzed seperately, and is intended to both understand how modeling was used -- and more importantly, to ensure that in the future, modeling efforts are responsive to the needs of hospital policy makers, clinicians, and other public health professionals.

Additionally, this project supported the work of two graduate researchers in the health sciences.

abstractText:
Resource management and conservation initiatives often require that communities work together to manage or conserve forests, grasslands, watersheds, and fisheries. While development partners emphasize scaling up the initiatives that work to new locations, we still understand little about when and why communities do or do not work together to manage or conserve, impeding successful scaling up and potentially leading to an inefficient use of donor dollars. This project, conducted in collaboration with a coastal community network that is funded by US Forest Service, unifies research from across academia and the development world to make concrete predictions about when and why communities work together in resource management. It will fund and train a postdoctoral researcher, a graduate student, and nine research team members in scientific research methods. The project will generate a set of guidelines for how development partners can select pilot sites where between-community cooperation is likely to succeed; with limited hurdles to cooperation, partners can then work out other obstacles to scaling up before expanding their initiatives.

This project investigates whether individuals’ concerns about what happens to neighboring communities, plus their connections with those communities, promotes successful resource management. Until now, ideas about what might promote between-community cooperation have remained largely theoretical and have usually been evaluated in the laboratory. This project involves on-the-ground data collection in 32 communities, where the project team will collect individual-level data about attitudes toward and connections with neighboring communities, as well as other candidate predictors of between-community cooperation, before the rollout of a fisheries management initiative. The team will then revisit these individuals to measure their participation in between-community cooperation 12 months after initiative rollout. By assessing the relevance of baseline factors to later successful resource management, this project provides a real-world test of theoretical work on when and why between-community cooperation works.

projectOutComesReport:
Sustainable resource management is a principal policy concern for the 21st century and is one of the UNDP's sustainable development goals. The end goal of sustainable management is for resources like forests and fish stocks to be available for future use, and a key concern is to get people to change their behavior in the present, like reducing how much wood or fish people take.

 

Many resource-management programs focus on community-based management: programs support local users to design and implement management programs that build on existing local leadership, institutions, and norms. These programs require the local users to work together, to benefit the entire community by protecting the resource. Work from academia, international organizations, and smaller nonprofits show that several things matter for sustainable use, like effective leadership and institutions, community participation in creating rules for how much people can take, and clearly designating who can and can’t use the resource.

 

This works well when there’s only one community involved, but many resources, like fisheries and forests are accessed by multiple communities. These basic principles do still apply – like effective leadership, working together to create rules, clear boundaries – but it can be harder to get people to work together on *anything*, including sustainable management, when more people are involved. Knowing how to better support collective action like this can potentially improve the design of initiatives meant to benefit multiple communities, whether those initiatives come from small nonprofits or even governmental or international organizations.

 

Based on our past work, we hypothesized that having more relationships that span community boundaries might improve participation in resource management. Research in anthropology, political science, psychology, conservation biology, and sociology has shown that these long-distance social relationships are often sources of (1) money, including for emergencies and for big expenditures; (2) information, including about new methods of farming or otherwise making money; and (3) trust, where knowing someone in another community means you know more about that community, including whether people there mean you harm or not. In other words, if you’re connected to people in other villages, neighborhoods, or towns, you not only know more about them, you also have outside sources of support and of information. Long-distance relationships can increase the value we place in people who live in other places.

 

Working in collaboration with a local nonprofit organization, we visited 28 fishing villages in 2022 and 2023 (Figure 1). These villages are split into five larger groups that are meant to work together on managing their fisheries – in other words, these are big fisheries accessible by multiple communities, making management harder. Our team asked 1317 people about their participation in fisheries management activities, their incomes and business activities, their social relationships, and whether they think local government is doing a good job with fisheries management.

 

First, we found support for previous findings on long-distance relationships and on sustainable management. Long-distance relationships promoted sustainable management by reducing conflict, sharing successful management strategies and opportunities for resource-based income (Pisor et al 2024), and providing large loans for new business expenses (Figure 2; Smith et al 2023). Individuals who thought local management was working better were more likely to participate in fisheries management (Smith et al 2024).

 

Second, we found that people with long-distance relationships were more likely to participate in fisheries management (Figure 3; Smith et al in press). People with more long-distance relationships were also more likely to trust other communities, which in turn also predicted greater participation – long-distance friends thus encouraged participation directly and indirectly by fostering trust. 

 

Intellectual merit. This work was the product of multiple disciplines and sectors, and is speaking back to those multiple disciplines and sectors. We have two published and one accepted paper so far, two in widely read journals: Conservation Letters and Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society: Biological Sciences. We also are working closely with our nonprofit partner to make these findings actionable, for initiatives in their organization and beyond. We’ve also brought these results to conferences of anthropologists, psychologists, and conservation biologists, with more planned in the near future.


Broader impacts. Beyond the applicability of these findings, this project has created training opportunities for five early-career researchers: one postdoc and four college graduates local to the study site – all four of whom are from a group underrepresented in the sciences. All five trainees received support and training in methods like individual interviews, focus groups, and experimental techniques that are regularly used in industry and the nonprofit sector, as well as in academia. Our project postdoc has gone on to an NIH (National Institutes of Health) funded postdoc in global health, while two of our four research assistants have gone on to complete master's degrees.

abstractText:
Viable processes for sustainable energy production must be environmentally benign, reduce green-house gas production, and utilize renewable resources. Under the Energy Independence Security Act of 2007, the U.S. has established a national goal of replacing 30% of petroleum-based fuels with plant-based lignocellulosic fuels by the year 2030. However, the efficiency of currently applied methods for the manufacturing of lignocellulosic biofuels is significantly hindered by the presence of lignin in the cell wall. Lignin, a polymer formed from the oxidative polymerization of monolignol and related compounds, shields cellulose from processing with hydrolytic enzymes, posing a major challenge to economically viable biofuel production. The proposed research will provide the fundamental knowledge necessary to tune the chemical composition of the cell walls of plants for optimal use in biofuel production. The broader impacts, beyond application to biofuel production, include the training of undergraduate and graduate students in multidisciplinary and quantitative methods.  

The accumulated knowledge resulting from this research will guide the formulation of efficient enzymes for the biosynthesis of lignin with properties that make it more amenable to biofuel production. The PIs target sorghum specifically, but the results will be generally applicable to most monolignol pathways in a majority of commercially important crop/forestry species. The study uses state-of-the-art single molecule methods, X-ray crystallography, spectroscopy, and thermochemical techniques to develop a detailed framework that describes critical oxidative steps within the monolignol biosynthetic pathway.  The work proposed will focus on: (1) protein-protein interaction between the P450s in the pathway (C4H, C3’H, and F5H) and their primary redox partner cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR), (2) the substrate specificity of the targeted P450s, (3) the effect of redox state and substrate-binding on the complex formation of P450-CPR and C4H-PAL. This study will provide the knowledge necessary to be able to tune the chemical composition of cell walls for use in biofuel and feedstock production.

projectOutComesReport:
The work was originally motivated by an urgent need to use plant biomass to produce liquid transportation fuels and chemicals that are currently made from petroleum. Under the Energy Independence Security Act of 2007, the U.S. has established a national goal of replacing 30% of petroleum-based fuels with lignocellulosic fuels by the year 2030. The investigated enzymes during the funding periods are key for the improvement of biofuel crop. Therefore our results from the NSF grant provided the knowledge necessary to be able to tune the chemical composition in cell walls for use in biofuel and chemical feedstock production. 

Upon execution of the proposed studies, the accumulated knowledge has guided us in formulating efficient enzymes in lignin biosynthesis. Our results, with its practical plant of choice, sorghum, could be generally applicable to most monolignol pathways in a majority of commercially important crop/forestry species. The contributing merit of our work is not only for the study of P450 enzymes and cell wall formation, but also to channel and/or target the pathway to metabolites which could find application in pathogen resistance of the plants in general. Therefore, our results aligns with to the scientific goals identified by NSF Energy for Sustainability with a key area of “Biomass Conversion, Biofuel & Bioenergy”. Processes for sustainable energy production must be environmentally benign, reduce green-house gas production, and utilize renewable resources.

There has been also great opportunity for both the community and society in the scientific knowledge gained from our successful completion of this project and its public dissemination. We recruited qualified students and provided extended support for research opportunities in our laboratories and to teach students how to disseminate scientific knowledge at scientific meetings and through publications.

abstractText:
Given the shortage of spectrum below 6GHz, millimeter wave (mmW) frequencies have played an important role in the emerging 5G networks and this trend is expected to continue in the next generations. Due to unfavorable propagation conditions and attenuation at high frequencies, mmW networks require the densification of base stations and radios equipped with a large number of antennas to compensate path loss via directional gain using narrow beams. The cost and power consumption of radios with antenna arrays present a significant challenge, and their architecture is of fundamental importance and influence on the entire networking stack. State-of-the-art approaches based on phased antenna array architecture are faced with several fundamental problems when radio bandwidth and the number of antennas increases including prohibitive latency in initial connectivity and link management, distortion in the directionality of the beams, reduced beamforming gain, and ability to suppress the interference in dense deployments. This project aims to develop and demonstrate a novel adaptive true-time-delay (TTD) based array for wideband mmW networks and overcome challenges of phased antenna arrays. The approach involves co-design and optimization of tunable radio frequency (RF) circuits, antenna array system, signal processing, and network protocols for low latency access, wideband beamforming gain, and interference management. 
  
The research work will pursue four key thrusts: Thrust 1 will develop TTD array-based fast beam training and spatial interference detection and estimation for mmW networks with large modulated bandwidth. The objective is to reduce the overhead in initial access due to beam training by exploiting frequency-dependent antenna weight vectors in TTD arrays through signal processing and develop a low latency protocol design for simultaneous beam training and interference estimation in dense mmW networks. Thrust 2 will focus on the data communication design using TTD arrays to facilitate multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) multiplexing and suppress interference from co-channel base stations and users. The main challenge is to achieve high beamforming gain over a wide modulated bandwidth together with effective nulling of wideband interferers. Thrust 3 will develop an experimental testbed for the evaluation of signal processing algorithms and protocols from Thrusts 1 and 2. It will involve the integration of widely reconfigurable delay compensating circuits and custom mmW front-end at 28GHz into a 16-element TTD antenna array. Thrust 4 will experimentally validate TTD array-based beam training, squint-free wideband beamforming and interference nulling, and wideband MIMO communications using the testbed developed in Thrust 3.

abstractText:
Polar bears live on sea ice that floats over the Arctic Ocean and that forms and melts each year within bays and among islands in eastern Canada.  This sea ice habitat is critical for providing polar bears a way to access seals, their primary prey. Polar bears hunt seals where they come up to breathe at holes in the ice and when they haul out onto the ice to have their pups.  The blubber of seals is the primary energy source for polar bears throughout the Arctic. A changing Arctic climate has already reduced the amount of sea ice that bears can use to access seals, and continued warming of several degrees over the next 100 years is expected to further decrease sea ice during the summer and early fall in many parts of the Arctic.  With less ice, polar bears across much of the Arctic are spending more time on land where they cannot access seals. Although polar bears have been observed feeding on nesting geese and seabirds, berries, and vegetation, these foods are more disbursed and less-energy rich than the typical prey of polar bears.  Thus, land-based foods may not occur in sufficient quality, quantity, or distribution to ensure the current widespread distribution of polar bears. This study seeks to better understand bear behavior on land and the degree to which land-based foods meet the energetic needs of polar bears.  The question of whether bears lose or maintain their body mass for extended periods on land is critical to determining potential effects of sea ice loss on birth and death rates – information that most Arctic nations need to manage their resident polar bears.  Because polar bears occur at the top of the Arctic food chain, they are also a key indicator species for changes in the Arctic as well as an iconic symbol of the effects of a changing climate. Our results will help identify actions to further protect this species and the communities whose cultures and safety are closely linked to the behavior of this Arctic predator.

The goals of this study are to determine the behavior and energetic balances of polar bears while summering on land.  We are proposing to 1) quantify the degree to which foods consumed while on land meet the energetic needs of polar bears and 2) thereby provide the information necessary to understand the implications of increasing warming, sea ice loss, and land use on polar bear well-being and population dynamics across the Arctic. We will do this by measuring energy expenditure, weight change, fat and protein composition of the weight change, activity and movement rates, and feeding behavior of males and females, young and old while they are on land. We will estimate the amount of energy coming from food as the difference between the energy expenditure measured with doubly labeled isotopic water and the energy released when body fat and protein are mobilized. If these values are equal, no useful energy is coming from food.  If the energy expenditure measured with doubly labeled water is higher than that available from mobilized protein and fat, then that difference is the amount of energy coming from ingested food. These measurements can only be done with the most advanced techniques available for human and animal research. These techniques include 1) GPS collars with built in video cameras that will allow us to accurately track bear movements and directly observe what they are doing and eating and 2) an isotopic water dilution technique that allows measurement of the number of calories they burn and how much fat and protein they gain or lose between two captures which will be about 21 days apart. These techniques will allow us to determine the implications of polar bears increasingly using land as their sea ice habitat continues to decline.  Thus, this study will provide information for understanding the future of polar bear populations, a significant part of Arctic food web, in a warming Arctic.

jrnl.artTitl: Polar bear energetic and behavioral strategies on land with implications for surviving the ice-free period
jrnl.auth: Pagano, Anthony M and Rode, Karyn D and Lunn, Nicholas J and McGeachy, David and Atkinson, Stephen N and Farley, Sean D and Erlenbach, Joy A and Robbins, Charles T

program: ARCTIC RESEARCH
projectOutComesReport:
Global warming is forecasted to result in a nearly ice-free Arctic during the summer as soon as mid-century. Because polar bears rely on sea ice to access their marine mammal prey, polar bears will be forced to spend less time hunting energy-dense marine mammals and more time in terrestrial environments consuming lower quality and more dispersed terrestrial foods. This has generated discussion about whether terrestrial foods, such as Arctic nesting waterfowl, could extend the duration that polar bears can survive on land without access to their marine mammal prey.

 

To answer this question, we measured the energy expenditure, diet, behavior, movement, and changes in body mass of 20 different polar bears on land and 12 different Arctic grizzly bears from August to September. We found polar bears on land exhibit varying behavioral strategies from being highly active and feeding on terrestrial foods to being highly sedentary and largely fasting. Those individuals that were largely fasting had reduced energy expenditures similar to hibernating grizzly bears, but 70% of the bears were more active and consumed terrestrial foods including berries, grasses, and bird carcasses. Yet, regardless of their feeding or energetic strategy, 19 of the 20 polar bears lost mass, losing an average of 1 kg per day (2.2 lbs per day), which indicates that continued increases in the duration on land will be associated with increased risk of starvation. In contrast, Arctic grizzly bears were even more active and fed intensively, primarily on waterfowl, ground squirrels, vegetation, and berries. However, these resources provided limited benefit in helping grizzly bears increase their body mass as they prepared for winter denning. The larger grizzly bears that overlapped with the body masses of smaller polar bears derived the least benefit from foraging.

 

The larger body size of polar bears allows them to be able to fast for extended durations, but also increases their overall energy expenditure while locating and foraging on terrestrial foods. This limits the net benefit of terrestrial foods in prolonging the period polar bears can survive without accessing their marine mammal prey. Ultimately, this study highlights that polar bears remain at risk of starvation with forecasted declines in Arctic sea ice and associated longer periods summering on land. Our next step is to use these data to predict the effects of forecasted sea ice loss on the reproduction and survival of specific polar bear populations in different parts of their range.

abstractText:
The project focuses on advances in synthesis techniques for zeolites – catalytic and molecular sieve materials used widely in the petroleum and chemical industries, and in environmental pollution control.  Specifically, the research focuses on understanding the process by which compounds known as organic structure directing agents (OSDAs) promote the growth of zeolite crystals that display specific physical and catalytic properties.  The investigators will integrate experiment and theory toward this goal, where cutting-edge simulation tools will be coupled with experimental measurements and advanced characterization techniques.  While the targeted zeolites are those used in diesel engine emissions control, the knowledge generated in the work will be broad-sweeping in scope. As such, the findings will have implications for renewable energy, improved technologies for advanced material production, and new approaches to generating intermediates/products in the pharmaceutical industry. The project incorporates educational and workforce training opportunities for graduate and undergraduate students, including cross-training of graduate students between the research groups.  Outreach activities will include interactive modules for K-12 outreach, a distance learning course related to emerging energy technologies, and new lab safety training modules for students.  All of those can be widely disseminated, adding to options for remote learning that will become more essential as the nation weathers the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The push for new energy sources has required an expansion in our understanding of fundamental chemistry. This is particularly true with respect to catalysis, with metal exchanged zeolites being actively utilized within industry. A significant roadblock to the further implementation of new zeolite catalysts is the general inability to control local structure such as active site spatial arrangement, a grand challenge problem in zeolite science. Recent work by one of the investigators’ research groups indicates that it is potentially possible to control the aluminum arrangement within the framework of a small pore zeolite (known as SSZ-39) by simply varying the relative amount of the cis and trans isomer of the organic structure directing agent used in synthesis. The research objective of the project is thus to guide the rational synthesis of zeolites with controlled active site arrangement by understanding the nucleation and growth of SSZ-39 from a faujasite zeolite. The central hypothesis of the project is that the nucleation and growth of SSZ-39, in an interconversion process from faujasite, is controlled by the dissolution of the faujasite, with the SSZ-39 forming at the faujasite/aqueous interface via heterogeneous nucleation off the dissolving faujasite crystal. Research efforts will focus on ways to control the aluminum arrangement in a system where all synthesis parameters (save the isomer ratio) are held fixed. However, the understanding—and potential for efficient design—of active site control in zeolites requires both experimental and computational methodologies, as zeolite synthesis is complex and cannot be adequately described without advances in the marriage of experimental and computational research activities. The project thus addresses a critical need to develop comprehensive, multi-scale models and to advance the understanding and value of predictive tools within the STEM pipeline.

abstractText:
This project will study how the spread of an infectious disease can affect the co-evolution of the pathogen and the host, and who those changes can create changes in the rest of the animal community. Emerging infectious diseases and the global loss of biodiversity are two leading challenges for the life sciences in the 21st century. Declines of the iconic Tasmanian devil in Australia represent an example of these two threats acting together to endanger a species. Additionally, as such large predators decline, the role of other species shifts in the food chain, which can lead to loss of biodiversity via secondary declines and extinctions of other species. These community changes can then feed back on the predator themselves, resulting in changes in developmental timing and reproduction. Thus, it is critical to study how losses of top predators lead to changes in food webs, population densities, and evolution of species with which they interact. Through outreach to the general public, this study will increase understanding of how infectious diseases affect biological communities and influence biodiversity. It will also provide training opportunities for US graduate students and post-doctoral scholars in an international setting.

Tasmanian devils and their fatal transmissible cancer, devil facial tumor disease (DFTD), represents an ideal study system to elucidate the impacts of top predator losses on community dynamics. The east to west spread of DFTD provides a rare, natural experiment to test how temporal variation in extent of devil declines across Tasmania affects community dynamics. Devils are indeed community architects, the declines of which cause the direct effects of mesopredator release that then cascades through the food web to indirect secondary declines of native species. The research will bridge ecological and evolutionary theory to predict how co-evolutionary interactions of devils and DFTD will affect current and future devil population densities. These predictions will then be plugged into (structural equation) models that incorporate field studies of ecological interactions within the Tasmanian devil food web across the decline gradient. Feedbacks of these community-level changes on Tasmanian devil life history evolution will be evaluated with genomic study of the basis of a rapid developmental trajectory and precocial breeding in female devils. Evolutionary feedbacks on mesopredators and prey will be assessed using landscape genomics studies to test the influence of variation in devil density on gene flow and adaptive potential across multiple generations.

projectOutComesReport:
Tasmanian devils are an iconic species, and they are threatened with extinction by a deadly, transmissible cancer called devil facial tumor disease, or DFTD. DFTD has spread across Tasmania in approximately 25 years, causing devil declines of up to 80% in many study sites. However, despite the lethality of the disease, devils persist in all study sites and even recover in some. The Tasmanian devil-DFTD study system is a rare, perhaps singular opportunity to study host-pathogen evolution in real time, with >25 years of population sampling data, as well as a natural experiment of east to west disease spread that resulted in populations being diseased for different generations. Long-term field study has facilitated study of population trends over many generations, thousands of genetic samples for detailed analysis of evolution across the genome, and the ability to study a species throughout its entire geographic range (Tasmanian devils only exist in Tasmania). Collectively, our work has shown that the devils show significant evidence of evolution throughout their genome, and that DFTD appears to be evolving to be less transmissible. The work we completed in this grant bridged ecology and evolution to study why devils are persisting, and how an eco-evolutionary perspective can provide new insights as to studying ecology or evolution alone.

Indeed, our mathematical models that bridged ecology and evolution show that devils are not doomed, as once thought, but rather show increased probability of persistence or co-existence with DFTD over the long term. These models are in contrast to early, simplified models showing devil extinction was inevitable, as well as later ecological models that showed lower chances of devil persistence. Previous work showed considerable genetic evidence for devil and DFTD evolution and coevolution, and the model predictions are consistent with real field data and time-series studies – a rare way to validate model predictions with long-term studies. In fact, in a world of human manipulation of endangered species for conservation purposes, our collective data shows that “do nothing” might be the most sensible approach because our collective, long-term insights show that devils and DFTD are evolving and coevolving. Alternative strategies, such as captive breeding and release of devils in zoos and wildlife parks to bolster natural population sizes are extremely costly and provide little benefit according to the models. Such strategies may even fuel the epizootic by introducing disease naïve devils.

The research supported under this award pushed the field of eco-evolutionary dynamics forward in three significant ways: 1) we were among the first to show that trophic cascades caused by top predator loss affected evolutionary dynamics of species at lower trophic levels by altering their population genomic structure; 2) we bridged ecology and evolution into eco-evolutionary models of coevolution in a host-pathogen system and showed that evolution plays a significant role in determining host persistence and host-pathogen coexistence when compared to ecological models alone; 3) we showed genomic evidence of coevolution between host and pathogen that explained significantly higher proportion of phenotypic variance explained that the genomics of host or pathogen alone. 

The work trained numerous early career professionals for career advancement for study of dentistry, medicine, nursing and computer science. Students and former researchers have also contributed to the American workforce, including at Biotech companies, Universities (as professors and postdoctoral researchers), in biomedical device development and sales and in nursing and pharmacy.

One of the most surprising and unexpected findings is that we discovered approximately 0.01% of devils that show spontaneous tumor regression in the wild, a phenomenon that is seen in 1 in 60,000-100,000 human patients. Using comparative whole genome sequencing, NSF-funded research led to discovery of a gene in the RAS family associated with tumor regression in Tasmanian devils. This mutation in DFTD turns on a tumor suppressor gene, which is homologous with that associated with colorectal cancer in humans. Upregulation of this gene in human colorectal cancer cells led to them outcompeting and causing apoptosis (programed cell death) in unmodified human colorectal cancer cells. We now have a provisional patent for this work, and results have led to a discovery with significant potential biomedical application. This work demonstrates that findings from basic research can lead remarkable discoveries that can lead to limitless potential for advancement of human health. Indeed 40% of all human medicine comes from animals and plants.

abstractText:
Both environmental and social factors are known to affect the timing of maturation at adolescence. Yet little is known about how these factors interact, vary with socioeconomic status, and differ for boys and girls. The aim of the current project is to disentangle the effects of nutrition and disease from several understudied factors on the timing of puberty in adolescents developing within contexts that present a wide range of social and environmental challenges. The project will study puberty as a set of physical, hormonal, and behavioral changes, allowing for a better assessment of factors affecting maturation in boys and girls. The research will address theoretical questions related to the evolution of the unique human pattern of growth and development. Insights from this work may also inform public health interventions related to adolescence. The project will train undergraduate and graduate students from under-represented minorities and will enhance research collaborations and infrastructures.

Theory and evidence suggest that individuals often accelerate development in response to cues of extrinsic mortality risk and decelerate development in response to disease or low energy availability. This project will examine the individual and combined effects of energy availability and cues of extrinsic mortality on the timing of puberty by longitudinally quantifying differences in the magnitude, tempo, and velocity of maturation across a diverse sample of youth facing a variety of different social and environmental stressors. It will employ a comprehensive set of measures in both boys and girls, including novel measures of male development (e.g., voice pitch), and conventional measures such as age at menarche, somatic growth, hormone levels, and self-reported Tanner stages. Research will be carried out in two locations with a wide range of variation in key measures to facilitate robust findings. Statistical models will be used to partition variation in measures of puberty into effects due to different social and environmental factors, and to assess whether measuring of the timing of puberty are associated with adolescents’ reproductive, educational, and life-course aspirations.

projectOutComesReport:
Project Outcomes Report for the General Public

This project investigated how the social and physical environment shapes the pace of human puberty. Adolescence is a critical period where the body “calibrates” itself to its environment, yet most research on puberty comes from wealthy, industrialized populations. To address this gap, this project established a longitudinal study on the island of Utila, Honduras—a unique "natural laboratory" where children from diverse backgrounds live in close proximity but experience different social and economic conditions. Over the course of three years, the project recruited 355 participants (ages 5–18) and 196 caregivers, collecting data on growth, hormones, voice pitch, immune function, and social networks to understand the biology of growing up. Key findings include:

  • Disentangling stress vs. energy: A central debate in child development is whether early maturation is driven by "psychosocial stress" or "energy availability" (calories/nutrition). By statistically disentangling these factors, our results demonstrated that distinct biological systems track different environmental signals. For example, while blood pressure was strongly predicted by energy availability (body fat percentage), markers of immune/oxygen load (hematocrit) were predicted by household instability. This challenges the field to identify which specific environmental cues drive specific physiological trade-offs
  • Validation of voice pitch as a biomarker: We successfully validated digital voice pitch analysis as a quantitative marker of male puberty. Historically, male puberty has been difficult to study because boys lack a distinct milestone like menarche (a girl's first period). We confirmed that vocal frequency tracks closely with testosterone and growth, establishing a scalable, non-invasive method for assessing male maturation in remote field sites.
  • Hormones, networks, and disgust: We mapped how puberty influences social behavior:
    • Social networks: We characterized kin and non-kin networks to identify variables that predicted social behavior. For example, as boys aged, their testosterone levels significantly predicted the size of their non-kin social networks, suggesting that rising androgens facilitate social expansion.
    • Disgust sensitivity: We also characterized disgust sensitivity across ages. We found that puberty does not recalibrate the "behavioral immune system," challenging the theory that pathogen avoidance fluctuates with reproductive maturation.
  • Migration and decision-making: In collaboration with developmental psychologists, we found that the experience of migration shapes cognitive development. Children who had immigrated to the island exhibited a generalized preference for high-risk options in a gambling task, whereas children born locally were better able to calibrate their risks. This implies that migration history may alter how children navigate risk-reward trade-offs.
  • Signaling need: We found that emotional behaviors (like crying) serve as honest biological signals. Children who displayed these signals more frequently were accurately perceived as "needier" by adults and received more parental investment, supporting evolutionary theories of parent-offspring communication.

Impact on Society beyond Science and Technology (Broader Impacts)

Establishment of the "Utila Child Health Project" (UCHP) longitudinal repository: The primary tangible outcome of this grant is the creation of the Utila Child Health Project, a permanent research infrastructure and longitudinal dataset. Unlike cross-sectional snapshots, this repository tracks 355 children and adolescents with biometric, hormonal, and social data over a 3-year period. This dataset now serves as a resource for anthropologists to test hypotheses regarding developmental plasticity in a non-WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) population.

Holistic support and ethical fieldwork models: Beyond scientific data, the project pioneered a "Data Camp" operational model that provided immediate tangible benefits, demonstrating that rigorous longitudinal research can function simultaneously as a community service program. In response to local needs, we integrated data collection with the provision of nutritious meals, childcare, and arts education provided by local teachers. This approach not only facilitated recruitment but served as a vital resource for working families facing food insecurity.

Human capital and the scientific pipeline: The project served as an incubator for eight early-career scientists, resulting in tangible career milestones for trainees:

  • Grant success: Undergraduate researchers leveraged the project’s infrastructure to secure their own independent funding, including multiple undergraduate research awards. Graduate students successfully secured REG, DDRIG, and NRT funding from NSF, and early fieldwork data helped secure six additional funding sources.
  • Leadership training: Graduate students served as field directors, gaining management experience in international logistics, personnel supervision, and community relations—skills rarely taught in the classroom.
  • Publication record: Trainees were the lead authors on the majority (16/18) of the project's manuscript and conference presentations.

Public health monitoring: The project successfully pivoted to address community-identified needs, resulting in a pilot study that identified that 52% of household water samples contained detectable levels of PFAS.

Sustainable health literacy tools: The project partnered with a local physician to provide full blood counts and created lasting educational infrastructure in the form of plain-language medical guides and visualized growth trajectories.

Participatory action research assets: Through the implementation of a Photo-voice protocol, the project involved children as "co-researchers," generating a visual and qualitative archive of how children perceive environmental health risks.

abstractText:
The ability to appropriately match an emotional response to cues in the environment begins developing during infancy and is critical to mental health and well-being throughout the life span. Infants learn to approach positive stimuli, such as smiling at happy faces, and avoid dangerous or threatening stimuli, such as turning away from angry faces. The goal of the proposed research is to understand the brain basis of approach and avoidance processes during infancy and the role of parent-child interactions in how those processes develop into childhood. This research will advance our understanding of approach and avoidance in the brain and how interactions between parents and infants influence their development. This proposed research will bring together early childhood specialists, students, parents and researchers to build a community around the study of early brain and cognitive development. 

The study will measure approach and avoidance behaviors in 6- to 12-month-old infants by observing their responses to positive and fearful stimuli and by parent-report of infants’ behavior in their home. The study will follow these children until they are age 4 when approach and avoidance behaviors as well as children’s decision-making will be measured. At both points in development, the study will record children’s brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique used to record the brain’s electrical activity to understand how individual differences in brain activity are related to development of approach and avoidance as well as how parent-child interactions might influence them. The proposed research will provide a new understanding of how approach and avoidance processes are shaped in early development and may shed light on how we can help people develop healthy emotion regulation beginning in infancy.

title: Probing the origins of approach and avoidance processes: brain, behavioral, and contextual factors

abstractText:
This project is about self-regulation, critical to wide ranging developmental outcomes across the lifespan. We know little about the origins and initial development of these skills during the first two years of life. It is during infancy, however, that behavioral and neurophysiological underpinnings of emotion reactivity, the precursor of regulation, are manifested. Moreover, sex differences in these foundational mechanisms have not been examined, despite considerable evidence of more advanced early regulation for girls. This research provides an intensive behavioral and brain activity examination of emotion reactivity, making connections with emerging self-regulation. Our study is the first to examine: (1) development of brain activity linked with fear/approach and related information processing biases across infancy, relying on emotion-eliciting tasks; (2) sex differences in brain activity changes across infancy, correspondence between behavioral and brain activity change patterns, and the extent to which these predict self-regulation around the 2nd birthday. Identified connections between reactivity and regulation will inform existing developmental theories and results will be disseminated to parents and early childhood educators, maximizing support for emerging child self-regulation.

Starting in infancy, regulation is supported by attentional capacity and becomes essential to functioning across most areas of life. Despite this importance, the origins of self-regulation are still poorly understood, especially with respect to the emotional underpinnings. Emotional reactivity “comes online” first, creating a foundation for subsequent development of regulatory capacity. Thus, growth in the principal domains of reactivity (fear and approach) in infancy, and links between these developmental changes and emerging self-regulation, require further study. We will answer lingering questions regarding how fearfulness and approach orientation on the behavioral and brain activity level are interrelated, and the extent to which these characteristics set the stage for self-regulation. We will leverage electroencephalography (EEG) recordings and multiple evaluations across the first two years of life to discern how changes in fear and approach contribute to the development of attention-based self-regulation, and how these processes may differ for boys and girls. As a result, parents and educators can be instructed regarding developmental periods during which effective negotiation of extreme changes in child approach or avoidance are particularly important from the standpoint of promoting regulation.

projectOutComesReport:
Executive Summary

This collaborative project between Washington State University (WSU) and Virginia Tech (VT) successfully completed longitudinal data collection across infancy and toddlerhood.  The WSU site recruited 62 families collecting EEG, behavioral, and parent-report data. Key accomplishments include harmonized protocols, preliminary findings on infant distress and temperament, and integration of datasets for longitudinal modeling. Broader impacts involve community outreach, partnerships with local organizations, and educational integration. Dissemination efforts span scientific conferences, community engagement, and plans for open-source code sharing. Training opportunities provided extensive STEM education for students, including EEG and behavioral coding, statistical modeling, and mentorship. 

Accomplishments

This WSU/VT collaborative project aimed to identify developmental shifts in EEG and behavioral markers of fear and approach during infancy and their links to emerging self-regulation in toddlerhood. Despite pandemic-related delays, the team successfully completed longitudinal data collection across six time points (6, 10, 14, 18, 22, and 26 months). Recruitment efforts yielded robust samples at both sites, with 62 families (33 girls, 29 boys) participating for the WSU portion of the project, and the overall sample enabling proposed analyses.

Major accomplishments include:
- Harmonization of EEG and behavioral protocols across sites through joint training and regular team meetings.
- Completion of EEG recordings, behavioral observations, and parent-report questionnaires during infancy, followed by effortful control assessments in toddlerhood.
- Integration of datasets from both sites and initiation of longitudinal modeling to test hypotheses regarding emotional reactivity and regulation.

Preliminary findings presented at conferences highlight:
- Variability in infant distress responses across fear-eliciting episodes, suggesting these contexts are not interchangeable
- Moderating effects of infant temperament on associations between maternal stress and sleep outcomes
- Birth order effects on the relationship between maternal anxiety and infant negative emotionality.

These results advance theoretical models of early emotional development and inform strategies for promoting regulatory capacity.

Societal Benefits / Broader Impacts

The project addresses a critical developmental question: how early emotional reactivity and regulation emerge and interact. Findings have significant implications for early intervention and parental guidance. By identifying precursors of self-regulation in the first years of life, this research supports low-cost strategies to foster healthy emotional development, reducing risk for later psychopathology and academic challenges.

Broader impacts include:
- Community Outreach: Newsletters summarizing findings were distributed through local family networks and child-focused organizations. Partnerships with Pullman Regional Hospital and Whitman County Library System facilitated dissemination.
- Future Engagement: Planned presentations at events such as the Palouse Pregnancy and Parenting Fair will extend impact beyond academia, benefiting parents, educators, and healthcare providers.
- Educational Integration: Project-related scholarship is incorporated into undergraduate and graduate coursework, enhancing student learning about developmental science and research methodology. 

Dissemination

Results have been disseminated through multiple channels:
- Scientific Conferences: Presentations at the International Congress on Infant Studies Conference and the Michael D. Griswold Symposium on Reproductive Health (2025) showcased findings related to observational methodology, birth order, maternal mental health, and infant temperament, as well as temperament’s role in sleep outcomes.
- Community Engagement: Updates provided to recruitment partners and local organizations; outreach events scheduled for early 2026.
- Future Plans: Manuscripts are in preparation for peer-reviewed journals. Annotated code for advanced statistical modeling will be made publicly available via GitHub and the University of Maryland CILVR repository, promoting methodological innovation in developmental science.

 

Opportunities for Training and Professional Development

The project provided extensive STEM training for undergraduate and graduate students, including:
- EEG acquisition and processing using the HAPPILEE pipeline
- Behavioral observations and coding with Noldus software
- Advanced statistical techniques for longitudinal modeling.

Students gained experience in hypothesis development, data analysis, and scientific writing, culminating in conference presentations. Graduate students mentored undergraduates, fostering leadership and pedagogical skills. Collaborative workshops on EEG preprocessing and mixture modeling further enhanced professional development. These experiences prepared trainees for careers in research, clinical practice, and academia.

Impact

This project contributes to developmental science by refining models of emotional reactivity and regulation and introducing methodological advances in EEG and behavioral data integration. Broader impacts extend to clinical child psychology, pediatrics, and early education, as findings inform strategies to support regulatory capacity during early childhood. Infrastructure improvements, including upgraded laboratory space and adoption of Noldus software, benefit future research efforts. Data and code will be shared publicly, promoting transparency and replication.

abstractText:
Scientists use radio observations of the sky to understand the evolution of galaxies and cosmic structures and answer questions about the origins of the universe. Cellular devices and other wireless technologies are vital to a modern economy but interfere with sensitive astronomical instruments. This project will develop technologies that will allow wireless devices and networks to coexist with scientific uses of the radio spectrum. These technologies include innovations in electronic systems that will make astronomical receivers more immune to interference from wireless devices; and advanced networking methods that allow wireless devices to intelligently cooperate with scientific observatories. 
This project includes both fundamental technical innovations and integrative system-level validation. It combines technical innovation at the passive receiver with new ideas on active transmitter management and looks at the problem in an integrative way. Technical innovations include novel hardware architecture and custom analog circuits, machine-learning-inspired design framework, cooperative wireless network protocol design, and testbed verification and evaluation. Breakthroughs in wideband beamforming, beam nulling, and interference cancellation through wideband true-time-delay arrays are proposed, which have the potential to enhance US competitiveness in various markets. A software-defined physical layer protocol brings a new approach to communication between active and passive devices, allowing for coordination between the device types. Industry interaction will enable the discussion of the practicality of ideas, placement of students in internships and permanent positions, and technology transfer. The astronomy application is a significant draw for women and minority engineering students and will allow for a significant increase in the diversity of the students involved in the project relative to historical norms in the engineering discipline. The proposed work will potentially impact the design and conception of future astronomy systems as wideband beamforming and cooperative network protocols will be available to technical standardization committees to enable practical coexistent deployment of active and passive services. The PIs' collaborations with astronomical observatories will allow for knowledge transfer and possible technology adoption in current and future instrument projects.

projectOutComesReport:
Modern science and technology increasingly rely on the ability to observe, process, and interpret extremely weak signals in environments crowded with interference. This project addressed a fundamental challenge faced by large antenna array systems: how to accurately receive wideband signals while suppressing strong interference and maintaining precise timing alignment across many antennas. The research focused on developing energy-efficient true-time-delay (TTD) array beamforming circuits that enable robust signal processing under realistic operating conditions.

A central outcome of the project was the successful development and experimental validation of several integrated circuit building blocks that together enable high-performance TTD array beamforming. These included compact power amplifiers, low-jitter clock generation circuits, tunable interference-rejection filters, and high-resolution delay compensation circuits. Each of these components was designed, fabricated, and measured in advanced semiconductor technologies, demonstrating that practical, scalable solutions are achievable within tight power and area constraints.

One of the project’s key intellectual contributions was the demonstration of tunable, interference-resilient front-end circuits that can adapt to changing spectral environments. The research team developed multi-stage notch filters based on switched-capacitor architectures that can dynamically suppress narrowband interferers without degrading desired signals. These filters were fabricated and tested, showing strong interference rejection while consuming very low power and occupying minimal chip area. Such capabilities are essential for array systems that must operate reliably in shared or congested spectrum.

Equally important was the development of precise timing and delay control circuits. True-time-delay beamforming requires that signals arriving at different antennas be aligned with extremely fine resolution. To achieve this, the project introduced low-power phase interpolators and multi-phase clock generators capable of producing accurate timing signals over wide frequency ranges. These circuits achieved high resolution and low jitter while avoiding the complexity and power overhead of conventional timing solutions. Measurement results confirmed their suitability for large-scale array systems, where small timing errors can significantly degrade overall performance.

The project also advanced the integration of machine learning techniques into circuit design. Novel Bayesian optimization algorithms were developed and applied to optimize complex circuit trade-offs involving power, performance, and robustness. By intelligently guiding simulation and design choices, these methods significantly reduced design time and computational cost. This cross-disciplinary contribution extends beyond beamforming systems and provides a powerful framework for optimizing complex engineering designs more broadly.

Beyond technical advances, the project made strong contributions to workforce development and education. Graduate and undergraduate students were deeply involved in all phases of the research, from system-level modeling and circuit design to silicon measurement and data analysis. Students gained hands-on experience with advanced laboratory equipment and learned how theoretical concepts translate into working hardware. Many students contributed to peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations, preparing them for careers in high-technology industries, academia, and national laboratories.

The results of this project were widely disseminated to both academic and industrial communities. Research findings were presented at leading international conferences and published in top-tier journals, ensuring broad visibility and long-term impact. In addition, the work was shared through an NSF Industry–University Cooperative Research Center, providing direct engagement with industry partners and facilitating knowledge transfer. These interactions helped ensure that the research remained grounded in real-world needs while influencing future technology development.

From a broader perspective, the project contributes to society by enabling more reliable and efficient sensing and communication systems in increasingly complex electromagnetic environments. By improving interference resilience and timing accuracy, the developed technologies support scientific discovery and advanced engineering systems that depend on precise signal reception. The project also demonstrates the value of combining circuit innovation, system-level thinking, and data-driven optimization to solve challenging problems at the intersection of hardware and algorithms.

In summary, this project delivered a set of experimentally validated technologies that advance the state of the art in true-time-delay array beamforming, trained a new generation of engineers and researchers, and strengthened collaboration between academia and industry. The outcomes provide a strong foundation for future research and practical deployment, exemplifying the National Science Foundation’s mission to promote scientific progress while delivering broad societal benefits.

abstractText:
With the maturing of mobile sensing, computing, and machine learning, scientists can now build intelligent tools to better understand human behavior by analyzing data from commercial, wearable sensors (such as smartwatches). The goal of this project is to design, build, and evaluate novel algorithms that continuously sense, model, analyze, and interpret human behavior from smartwatch sensor data collected continuously in the wild. Machine learning methods will be designed to infer behavior patterns from collected data as well as generate explanations of behavior patterns that can be easily interpreted by humans with diverse backgrounds. The computational methods will be evaluated using historical data as well as new data collected in free-living environments. The relationship between health and behavior will be explored by using machine learning to derive clinical health scores from collected and modeled sensor data.  The research will involve students from diverse disciplinary and demographic backgrounds through involvement in summer research programs and capstone projects.

The technical goals of this project are divided into three aims. First, because continuous behavior sensing requires resources that exceed the power capacity of current smartwatches, the investigators will design algorithms that optimize the trade-off between predictive performance and power consumption. Second, the investigators will create robust behavior models that combine sparse label information with sensor data to automatically construct a vocabulary of human behavior, and employ domain adaptation to generalize models across people, times, and behavior types. Third, the investigators will create machine learning methods to produce accurate and interpretable clinical health scores from behavior data with automatically-generated text explanations.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
